name: Debugging Lab Learn
title: Debugging Curriculum & Mastery Guide
description: Master debugging fundamentals, error diagnosis, data structure bugs, algorithm pitfalls, and language-specific troubleshooting.

sections.title: Debugging Fundamentals
sections.description: Core concepts, mindsets, and distinction between bugs and errors in software development.

lessons.title: What is Debugging?
lessons.description: Learn what debugging is, how it fits into the development cycle, and the systematic process of finding bugs.

content.text: Debugging is the systematic process of identifying, analyzing, and resolving bugs, flaws, or unexpected behaviors in computer software or hardware. Named after the physical removal of a moth from a Harvard Mark II computer relay in 1947 by Admiral Grace Hopper's team, debugging transforms faulty code into functional software.

When code runs, it follows a strict sequence of instructions. If the output disagrees with expectations, a bug exists. Debugging involves isolating the line or state where the software's execution diverges from the intended logic.

Writing code is only 30% of software engineering; 70% is spent reading, testing, and debugging code. Strong debugging skills dramatically reduce feature delivery time and prevent critical runtime failures in production.

content.title: Calculating Average of Numbers
content.description: Computing the average of two numbers with operator precedence bug.
content.whyItFails: In mathematics and programming, division (/) has higher precedence than addition (+). Thus `a + b / 2.0` calculates `a + (b / 2.0)`. For inputs 10 and 20, it evaluates as 10 + 10.0 = 20.0.
content.explanation: Adding parentheses `(a + b)` forces addition to evaluate first before division, producing `(10 + 20) / 2.0 = 30 / 2.0 = 15.0`.

items.title: Reproduce the Bug
items.description: Consistently recreate the failure using minimal test inputs.

items.title: Isolate the Cause
items.description: Locate the specific function or statement causing unexpected behavior.

items.title: Apply the Fix
items.description: Modify the code to fix the logic without breaking other features.

items.title: Verify & Regression Test
items.description: Confirm the fix with edge cases and run past test suites.

content.title: Pro Tip
content.text: Never guess where a bug is. Use print statements, loggers, or debuggers to inspect actual runtime values.

keyTakeaways: Debugging is a methodical process of finding why runtime behavior differs from expected logic.
Always isolate variables and reproduce bugs with simple test cases.
Operator precedence and type conversion errors are extremely common beginner bugs.

quiz.question: What is the primary objective of debugging?
options: To rewrite the entire codebase from scratch
To systematically find, analyze, and correct flaws in software
To convert high-level code into assembly code
quiz.explanation: Debugging is the systematic process of finding, analyzing, and correcting bugs or unwanted behavior in software.

lessons.title: Why Debugging is Important
lessons.description: Understand the financial, performance, and reliability impacts of debugging in software engineering.

content.text: Software powers critical systems—from banking transactions to medical devices. Unchecked bugs lead to software crashes, security vulnerabilities, and significant financial loss.

items: Ensures Reliability: Guarantees software behaves accurately under all valid conditions.
Improves Security: Many security exploits (e.g. buffer overflows, SQL injection) stem from unhandled edge-case bugs.
Enhances Performance: Debugging bottlenecks reduces CPU and memory usage.
Saves Engineering Time: Quick debugging workflows reduce feature development cycles.

keyTakeaways: Debugging prevents system downtime and security vulnerabilities.
Mastering debugging makes you a significantly faster problem solver.

quiz.question: Which of the following is a direct benefit of effective debugging?
options: Increased software reliability and reduced runtime crashes
quiz.explanation: Effective debugging increases software reliability and eliminates runtime crashes before production.

lessons.title: Bug vs Error
lessons.description: Learn the crucial differences between errors, bugs, faults, and failures in computing.

rows: A mistake or misconception made by a human developer in thought or syntax.
The flaw or defect in the source code caused by an error.
An observable incorrect runtime behavior or crash when executing code.

content.text: In short: Humans make Errors, which introduce Bugs in code, resulting in system Failures during execution.

keyTakeaways: Errors are human mistakes during coding.
Bugs are static code defects resulting from errors.
Failures are runtime manifestations of bugs.

quiz.question: What is the relation between error, bug, and failure?
options: A failure leads to a bug, which creates an error
An error is made by a developer, creating a bug in code, leading to a failure at runtime
Bugs are hardware issues; errors are software issues
They are exact synonyms with no distinction
quiz.explanation: Errors are human mistakes, bugs are defects in code, and failures are observable execution errors.

lessons.title: Debugging Mindset
lessons.description: Develop the analytical mindset required to systematically solve complex programming bugs.

items: Observe: Read the error message or observe faulty output.
Hypothesize: Formulate a guess about what variable or branch is incorrect.
Test: Add print statements, assertions, or breakpoints to test the hypothesis.
Conclude: Validate whether hypothesis was correct. Repeat if necessary.

content.title: Key Mindset Rule
content.text: Don't blame the compiler or language interpreter. The computer strictly executes what you wrote, not what you intended!

keyTakeaways: Treat debugging like a scientific experiment with hypotheses and tests.
Be patient and break complex problems into small testable units.

quiz.question: What is the first step in the scientific debugging process?
options: Change random lines of code until it works
Observe the error message and reproduce the faulty behavior
quiz.explanation: The first step is observing the problem clearly and reproducing the exact failure.

sections.title: Types of Errors
sections.description: Syntax, compilation, runtime, logical, wrong answer, TLE, and MLE errors.

lessons.title: Syntax Errors
lessons.description: Recognize and fix grammar violations of programming language rules.

content.text: A syntax error occurs when source code violates the grammar rules of the programming language. The compiler or interpreter cannot parse the source file.

content.title: Missing Semicolon / Parenthesis
content.whyItFails: Missing trailing semicolons in C++/Java or missing colons/closing parentheses prevents compiler parsing.
content.explanation: Adding required colons, closing braces, and semicolons restores valid language syntax.

keyTakeaways: Syntax errors occur before code execution during parsing.
Carefully check line numbers reported by compilers.

quiz.question: When are syntax errors caught?
quiz.explanation: Syntax errors prevent code from compiling or being parsed, caught before execution begins.

lessons.title: Compilation Errors
lessons.description: Type mismatches, undeclared symbols, missing imports, and linker errors.

content.text: Compilation errors happen when code is syntactically valid but fails static type checking, variable declaration resolution, or linking in compiled languages like C++, Java, or Rust.

content.title: Undeclared Variable & Type Mismatch
content.whyItFails: C++ requires all variables to be declared with a type. Java strictly enforces type matching during compilation.
content.explanation: Declare types explicitly and use conversion functions like Integer.parseInt for string conversion.

keyTakeaways: Static type checkers flag symbol and type mismatches at compile time.
Read compiler messages from top to bottom.

quiz.question: Which error occurs when assigning a String literal to an int variable in Java?
quiz.explanation: Java performs strict type checking during compilation, triggering a type mismatch compile error.

lessons.title: Runtime Errors
lessons.description: Null pointers, index out of bounds, divide by zero, and stack overflow exceptions.

items: NullPointerException / AttributeError: Accessing methods on an uninitialized/null reference.
IndexOutOfBoundsException / IndexError: Accessing array/list indices outside [0, length-1].
ArithmeticException: Division or modulo by zero.
StackOverflowError: Infinite recursion exceeding memory stack limit.

content.title: Index Out of Bounds Bug

buggyCode.python:
nums = [10, 20, 30]
for i in range(len(nums) + 1):  # Bug: IndexError when i = 3
    print(nums[i])

content.whyItFails: Arrays with length N have valid indices 0 to N-1. Index N is out of bounds.
content.explanation: Change loop bound condition from `i <= N` to `i < N` or `range(len(nums))`.

keyTakeaways: Runtime errors occur while the program is actively executing.
Always check boundary conditions before array indexing.

quiz.question: What exception occurs when accessing index 5 on an array of size 5?
quiz.explanation: Array indices are 0-based. An array of size 5 has valid indices 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. Index 5 causes IndexOutOfBounds.

lessons.title: Logical Errors
lessons.description: Subtle bugs where program compiles and runs without crashing but produces incorrect answers.

content.text: Logical errors are the hardest bugs to detect because the language compiler and interpreter raise zero warnings or exceptions. The program runs cleanly, but the logic produces wrong outputs.

content.title: Off-by-one and Incorrect Operator
content.whyItFails: 1. Initializing maxVal to 0 fails if array contains negative numbers (e.g. [-5, -2]). 2. Using `<` finds minimum instead of maximum.
content.explanation: Set initial maxVal to `arr[0]` and compare using `>` operator.

keyTakeaways: Logical errors produce incorrect results without throwing exceptions.
Initialize variables carefully using problem context or first elements.

quiz.question: Why are logical errors dangerous?
options: They prevent the code from compiling
They run cleanly without crashing, making output incorrect silently
quiz.explanation: Logical errors do not trigger crashes or syntax warnings, so incorrect results go unnoticed unless verified against test cases.

lessons.title: Wrong Answer
lessons.description: Diagnose why code fails specific competitive programming or assessment test cases.

items: Integer Overflow: Using 32-bit `int` when numbers exceed 2*10^9 (use `long long` / `long`).
Precision Loss: Comparing floating point numbers with `==` instead of threshold `abs(a - b) < 1e-9`.
Off-by-One Errors: Incorrect loop bounds (`<=` vs `<`).
Uninitialized State: Reusing global variables across multiple test cases without resetting.

keyTakeaways: Check for integer overflow on large input constraints.
Reset global or stateful variables for multiple test case inputs.

quiz.question: In C++, what causes `int` to wrap around to negative values when computing factorial of 20?
quiz.explanation: 32-bit signed integers overflow above ~2x10^9. Factorial of 20 requires a 64-bit `long long`.

lessons.title: Time Limit Exceeded
lessons.description: Identify suboptimal O(N^2) algorithms and infinite loops triggering TLE.

content.text: Time Limit Exceeded occurs when your solution takes longer than the allowed CPU time limit (usually 1.0 to 2.0 seconds, corresponding to ~10^8 operations in C++).

content.title: Infinite Loops
content.text: Missing loop increment statements (`i++`) cause infinite loops which immediately result in TLE.

keyTakeaways: Calculate operations based on input size N. Aim for <= 10^8 ops per second.
Verify loop termination variables update properly on every iteration.

quiz.question: An input constraint has N = 10^5. Which time complexity will likely cause TLE?
quiz.explanation: For N = 10^5, N^2 = 10^10 operations, exceeding the ~10^8 per second threshold.

lessons.title: Memory Limit Exceeded
lessons.description: Analyze memory complexity, large matrix allocations, and recursion stack overflow.

content.text: Memory Limit Exceeded happens when your program allocates more RAM than permitted (typically 256MB).

items: Over-allocation: Allocating static arrays like `int dp[10000][10000]` consumes 10000*10000*4 bytes = 400MB.
Memory Leaks: Allocating memory in loops without freeing (in C/C++).
Deep Recursion: Recursion depth exceeding stack space without tail optimization.

keyTakeaways: Calculate memory footprint before allocating large multi-dimensional arrays.
Optimize DP table space (e.g. reducing 2D DP to 1D array when possible).

quiz.question: How much RAM does a 2D integer array `int dp[5000][5000]` occupy in C++?
quiz.explanation: 5000 x 5000 = 25,000,000 integers. Each 4-byte int yields 100,000,000 bytes = ~100 MB.

sections.title: Debugging Workflow
sections.description: Structured workflows for reading error messages, stack traces, variable tracing, and print debugging.

lessons.title: Reading Error Messages
lessons.description: Learn how to decipher compiler and interpreter error outputs quickly.

content.code:
Main.java:14: error: cannot find symbol
        System.out.println(result);
                           ^
  symbol:   variable result
  location: class Main

items: File & Line Number: `Main.java:14` specifies exact file and line where compiler gave up.
Error Category: `cannot find symbol` indicates an undefined variable or method name.
Caret (^): Points to exact column where identifier was expected.

keyTakeaways: Always read the FIRST error message listed; subsequent errors are often cascading noise.
Locate file name, line number, and error type.

quiz.question: Why should you fix the first compiler error in a long list of errors first?
options: Later errors are often phantom errors caused by the first broken line
Compilers ignore the first error anyway
First errors are always warning messages
It makes no difference which order you fix errors
quiz.explanation: Compilers can get out of sync after the first error, generating cascading false errors below it.

lessons.title: Stack Traces
lessons.description: Navigate call stacks to locate execution crashes across multi-function programs.

content.text: A stack trace lists active function calls at the exact moment an exception occurred. Call frames are stacked top-to-bottom or bottom-to-top.

content.code:
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NullPointerException
	at com.app.Service.processUser(Service.java:42)
	at com.app.Controller.handleRequest(Controller.java:18)
	at com.app.Main.main(Main.java:8)

content.text: Look for your custom application code lines first, rather than standard library or framework lines.

keyTakeaways: Top-most frame in stack trace shows where the crash occurred.
Filter out third-party framework lines to locate your custom code.

quiz.question: In a stack trace, where is the immediate site of the exception located?
options: At the top-most line of the stack trace call stack
At the very bottom of the trace
quiz.explanation: The top-most call frame indicates the precise method and line number where the exception was thrown.

lessons.title: Variable Tracing
lessons.description: Construct execution trace tables to track state changes line-by-line.

content.text: A trace table tracks values of variables at every step of execution.

keyTakeaways: Use pen and paper or a spreadsheet trace table to trace loop state changes.
Essential for understanding recursion and nested loops.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of a variable trace table?
options: To record variable values step-by-step through execution
quiz.explanation: A trace table records variable states after every line/iteration to verify state transitions.

lessons.title: Print Debugging Workflow
lessons.description: Systematic insertion of structured print statements for fast local debugging.

content.text: Avoid plain `print(x)`. Instead, print variable names, loop indices, and context labels:

content.code:
# Bad:
print(val)

# Good:
print(f"[DEBUG] idx={i}, val={val}, current_sum={total_sum}")

content.title: Clean Up
content.text: Always remove or disable print statements before submitting code to production or online judges.

keyTakeaways: Include context labels and iteration counts in debug print statements.
Remove debug logs prior to final code submission.

quiz.question: Which print statement is most effective for debugging?
quiz.explanation: Labeled print statements showing variable names, values, and execution steps provide clear context.

sections.title: Debugging Patterns
sections.description: Identify and resolve recurring bugs in loops, conditions, variables, and function calls.

lessons.title: Loops
lessons.description: Debug off-by-one errors, infinite loops, and boundary condition failures in for/while loops.

items: Off-By-One (OBOE): Iterating `i <= len` instead of `i < len`.
Stale Loop Condition: Forgetting to increment counter in while loop (`while(i < n)` without `i++`).
Incorrect Termination: Using wrong comparison operators (`>` vs `>=`).

content.title: Infinite Loop Bug

buggyCode.python:
i = 0
while i < 5:
    print(i)
    # Bug: forgot i += 1, infinite loop!

correctCode.python:
i = 0
while i < 5:
    print(i)
    i += 1  # Corrected

content.whyItFails: Loop counter `i` is never modified inside loop body, causing `i < 5` to remain true infinitely.
content.explanation: Increment `i` on each loop iteration to reach loop termination condition.

keyTakeaways: Verify that loop counters approach the termination condition every iteration.
Watch out for 0-based vs 1-based index boundaries.

quiz.question: What happens if a while loop condition never evaluates to false?
options: Infinite Loop (resulting in TLE or crash)
quiz.explanation: If loop condition never becomes false, execution loops endlessly until terminated or killed by TLE.

lessons.title: Conditions
lessons.description: Debug assignment in condition, boolean operator precedence, and dangling else bugs.

content.title: Assignment vs Comparison
content.whyItFails: Using `=` assigns 10 to `x`. Since 10 is non-zero, condition evaluates to true every time.

keyTakeaways: Use `==` for comparison, not `=`.
Parenthesize complex boolean conditions: `(a && b) || c`.

quiz.question: In C/C++, what is the result of `if (x = 0)`?
options: Assigns 0 to x and evaluates condition as false
quiz.explanation: `x = 0` assigns 0 to `x`. Since 0 is treated as false in boolean context, condition evaluates to false.

lessons.title: Variables
lessons.description: Uninitialized variables, variable shadowing, global scope contamination, and type coercion bugs.

content.text: Variable shadowing occurs when an inner block declares a variable with the same name as an outer variable, hiding the outer variable.

keyTakeaways: Avoid re-declaring variables with identical names in nested blocks.
Always initialize local variables before reading them.

quiz.question: What is variable shadowing?
options: Declaring an inner variable with the same name as an outer variable, obscuring access to outer variable
quiz.explanation: Shadowing occurs when an inner scope variable hides an outer variable of the same name.

lessons.title: Functions
lessons.description: Pass-by-value vs pass-by-reference bugs, missing return values, and side effects.

content.title: Swap Function in C++
content.whyItFails: Passing by value creates copies of `a` and `b`. Swapping local copies leaves caller variables unchanged.
content.explanation: Use reference `&a, &b` in C++ or pass mutable objects/pointers to modify original caller data.

keyTakeaways: Primitive types are passed by value in C++/Java/Python.
Ensure functions return values on all execution control branches.

quiz.question: Why does `swap(a, b)` fail to modify original variables when parameters are passed by value?
options: The function operates on local copies of variables rather than original memory locations
quiz.explanation: Pass-by-value copies variable values into new local memory frames; changes do not affect original variables.

sections.title: Data Structure Debugging
sections.description: Debug common pitfalls in Arrays, Strings, Hashing, Linked Lists, Stacks, Queues, Trees, and Graphs.

lessons.title: Array Debugging
lessons.description: Troubleshoot off-by-one indices, sub-array bounds, and array modification during iteration.

items: Valid Index Range: `0` to `array.length - 1`.
Two Pointer Bugs: `left` and `right` pointers crossing each other (`left <= right` vs `left < right`).
Prefix Sum Bounds: `prefix[r] - prefix[l-1]` handling for `l = 0`.

keyTakeaways: Check bounds for empty arrays (length == 0).
Be cautious when modifying array size while iterating.

quiz.question: What is the correct 1D array index range for an array with N elements?
quiz.explanation: Standard zero-indexed arrays span indices 0 up to N - 1.

lessons.title: String Debugging
lessons.description: Immutability, substring index bounds, character encoding, and string comparison.

content.title: Java / Python String Modification
content.whyItFails: Strings in Java and Python are immutable. `concat()` returns a new String without modifying original.
content.explanation: Reassign the returned string or use StringBuilder.

keyTakeaways: In Java/Python, Strings are immutable; reassign method return values.
Compare String contents with `.equals()` in Java, not `==`.

quiz.question: In Java, how should string contents be compared for equality?
quiz.explanation: `==` compares object references in memory. `str1.equals(str2)` checks character sequence content equality.

lessons.title: Hash Map & Hash Set Debugging
lessons.description: Troubleshoot hash key collisions, mutable keys, and missing custom hashCode/equals implementations.

items: Mutable Objects as Keys: Modifying an object after inserting into HashMap changes its hashCode, rendering it unreachable.
Missing Key Check: Calling `map.get(key)` for non-existent key returns `null` or throws KeyError.
Custom Objects: Classes used as HashMap keys MUST override both `equals()` and `hashCode()`.

keyTakeaways: Use immutable types (String, Integer, Tuple) as map keys.
Always check `map.containsKey(key)` or use `getOrDefault()` before accessing values.

quiz.question: What happens if you use a mutable object as a HashMap key and then modify the object?
options: Object becomes unreachable via `map.get()` because its hash code changed
quiz.explanation: Modifying key attributes alters its hash code, so subsequent `get()` queries look in wrong bucket.

lessons.title: Linked List Debugging
lessons.description: Fix NullPointerExceptions, lost pointer references, and infinite cycle loops in linked lists.

content.text: When updating pointers, changing `node.next` before preserving `node.next` breaks the list connection.

content.title: Dummy Head Node
content.text: Using a dummy head node (`ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0); dummy.next = head;`) simplifies edge cases when deleting/inserting head.

keyTakeaways: Store next node reference before overwriting `curr.next`.
Use dummy head nodes to avoid null checks for head operations.

quiz.question: Why is a dummy head node useful in linked list problems?
options: It handles edge cases at head insertion/deletion without special null checks
It converts linked list into array
quiz.explanation: Dummy nodes eliminate special edge-case branching when operating on the first list node.

lessons.title: Stack Debugging
lessons.description: Debug EmptyStackException, stack frame overflow, and monotonic stack boundary logic.

content.text: Calling `pop()` or `peek()` on an empty stack throws runtime exception. Always verify `!stack.isEmpty()` before access.

keyTakeaways: Always check `!stack.isEmpty()` before calling `pop()` or `peek()`.
Monotonic stack loops need clear comparison conditions (`<` vs `<=`).

quiz.question: Which check prevents EmptyStackException before calling `stack.pop()`?
quiz.explanation: Checking `!stack.isEmpty()` ensures elements exist prior to popping.

lessons.title: Queue Debugging
lessons.description: Troubleshoot BFS queue termination, null queue elements, and priority queue ordering.

content.text: In Breadth-First Search (BFS), mark nodes as visited *when pushing* to queue, NOT when popping. Pushing unvisited nodes causes duplicate queue insertions.

keyTakeaways: Mark nodes visited immediately when adding to BFS queue.
Specify custom comparator for PriorityQueue sorting behavior.

quiz.question: In BFS graph traversal, when should a node be marked as visited?
options: When pushing the node into the queue
When popping the node from the queue
At the very end of the function
quiz.explanation: Marking visited upon push prevents duplicate identical nodes from being queued repeatedly.

lessons.title: Tree Debugging
lessons.description: Debug base case recursion, binary search tree invariant violations, and null child references.
keyTakeaways: Ensure recursive tree traversals return explicit values for null roots.
Validate BST properties across range bounds `(min, max)`, not just immediate parent/child.

quiz.question: Why is comparing only `node.left.val < node.val < node.right.val` insufficient to validate a Binary Search Tree?
options: It fails to ensure descendants in left subtree are smaller than all ancestor nodes
quiz.explanation: BST property requires ALL nodes in left subtree to be smaller than ancestor, requiring range validation `(min, max)`.

lessons.title: Graph Debugging
lessons.description: Fix infinite recursion cycles in undirected graphs, disconnected components, and matrix bounds.

content.text: Undirected graphs create bidirectional edges (`u -> v` and `v -> u`). Traversal without a `visited` array causes infinite recursion/loops.

keyTakeaways: Always maintain `visited` set or array for cyclic graphs.
Check matrix boundary bounds (`r >= 0 && r < rows && c >= 0 && c < cols`) before grid access.

quiz.question: What happens if you run DFS on an undirected graph without a visited array?
options: Infinite recursion loop leading to StackOverflowError
quiz.explanation: Without tracking visited nodes, DFS bounces infinitely between adjacent connected nodes until stack overflow.

sections.title: Algorithm Debugging
sections.description: Debug Searching, Sorting, Recursion, Greedy, and Dynamic Programming algorithms.

lessons.title: Searching Algorithm Debugging
lessons.description: Debug Binary Search mid overflow, infinite loop bounds, and search space reduction.

content.text: Use `low <= high` when searching for exact element; use `low < high` for lower/upper bound predicate search.

keyTakeaways: Calculate `mid = low + (high - low) / 2` to prevent integer overflow.
Verify loop progress: ensure search space decreases every step.

quiz.question: Why is `mid = low + (high - low) / 2` preferred over `(low + high) / 2`?
options: It prevents integer overflow when `low + high` exceeds 32-bit integer limits
quiz.explanation: For large array indices, `low + high` can overflow 32-bit signed ints, producing negative mid values.

lessons.title: Sorting Algorithm Debugging
lessons.description: Troubleshoot comparator contract violations, non-stable sort bugs, and QuickSort pivot selection.

content.text: Custom comparators MUST satisfy strict weak ordering:

items: Irreflexive: `comp(a, a)` MUST return false.
Asymmetric: If `comp(a, b)` is true, `comp(b, a)` MUST be false.
Transitive: If `comp(a, b)` and `comp(b, c)` are true, `comp(a, c)` MUST be true.

content.title: Comparator Pitfall
content.text: Returning `>=` or `<=` in C++ `std::sort` comparator violates strict weak ordering and leads to segmentation faults!

keyTakeaways: Use strictly `<` or `>` in custom comparators, never `<=` or `>=` in C++.
Be aware of stability when sorting multi-attribute objects.

quiz.question: In C++, what occurs if custom comparator for `std::sort` returns `a <= b` instead of `a < b`?
options: Undefined behavior or Segmentation Fault due to strict weak ordering violation
quiz.explanation: `std::sort` requires strict weak ordering where `comp(a, a)` is false. Returning true for equal elements causes pointer out-of-bounds crashes.

lessons.title: Recursion Debugging
lessons.description: Trace stack overflow, missing base cases, and return value accumulation in recursive trees.

items: Base Case: Must exist and stop recursive invocation.
State Reduction: Each recursive call must move closer to base case.
Return Combination: Return values from recursive subproblems must combine correctly.

keyTakeaways: Draw a recursion tree diagram to visualize call stack depth.
Ensure every execution branch hits a defined base case.

quiz.question: What error occurs when a recursive function lacks a valid base case?
quiz.explanation: Without a base case, recursive calls continue indefinitely until stack memory is exhausted.

lessons.title: Greedy Algorithm Debugging
lessons.description: Identify non-optimal greedy choices, counterexamples, and proof of correctness.

content.text: Greedy algorithms make locally optimal choices. If problem lacks optimal substructure or greedy choice property, greedy yields wrong answers.

content.title: Coin Change Problem (Non-Greedy)

correctCode.cpp: // Use Dynamic Programming for Coin Change when coins are arbitrary

content.whyItFails: Greedy choice is not optimal for non-canonical coin systems.
content.explanation: Test greedy logic against small counterexamples. Switch to DP if counterexample exists.

keyTakeaways: Test greedy hypotheses with counterexamples before coding.
If locally optimal choice fails global optimum, switch to Dynamic Programming.

quiz.question: Why does greedy coin change fail for coins {1, 3, 4} and target amount 6?
options: Greedy chooses 4+1+1 (3 coins), whereas optimal choice is 3+3 (2 coins)
quiz.explanation: Greedy chooses highest coin 4 first, producing 3 coins instead of 2.

lessons.title: Dynamic Programming Debugging
lessons.description: Debug state definition, transition relation, base case initialization, and iteration order.

items: State Definition: What does `dp[i][j]` represent precisely?
Base Cases: Are `dp[0]` or boundary initializations accurate?
Transition Formula: Does `dp[i]` depend strictly on ALREADY solved subproblems?
Iteration Direction: Is bottom-up loop iterating in correct order (left-to-right vs right-to-left)?

keyTakeaways: Print small 1D or 2D DP tables to verify subproblem values.
Verify loop iteration direction fills dependent subproblems first.

quiz.question: In 0/1 Knapsack 1D space optimization, why must space loop iterate backwards `w = W down to weight[i]`?
options: To prevent using the same item multiple times in the same step
quiz.explanation: Iterating backwards ensures `dp[w - weight[i]]` references previous item state, preventing item re-use.

sections.title: Test Case Design
sections.description: Master test case design, boundary case identification, and edge case coverage.

lessons.title: Test Case Design Fundamentals
lessons.description: Learn equivalence partitioning, stress testing, and systematic test design.

content.text: Divide input domains into valid and invalid partitions. Test one representative input from each group.

keyTakeaways: Test small inputs, max inputs, zero/negative inputs, and duplicate inputs.
Stress test custom solutions against brute force implementations using random generators.

quiz.question: What is equivalence partitioning?
options: Testing every single integer from 1 to 1 billion
Dividing input domain into classes where program handles all elements in a class similarly
quiz.explanation: Partitioning groups similar inputs so testing one representative validates the entire group.

lessons.title: Boundary Cases
lessons.description: Identify limits: min/max constraints, array limits, and integer bounds.

items: Array Size Bounds: `N = 0`, `N = 1`, `N = max_limit` (e.g. 10^5).
Integer Limits: `INT_MIN`, `0`, `INT_MAX`, `10^18` for long long.
Graph Topology: Single node, disconnected graph, complete graph, linear line graph.

keyTakeaways: Always test `N = 0` and `N = 1` first.
Verify max input limits do not exceed data type limits.

quiz.question: Which of the following represents a boundary test case for an array function?
options: An empty array `N = 0` and single-element array `N = 1`
quiz.explanation: Limits `N = 0` and `N = 1` test boundary handling where standard loop logic often fails.

lessons.title: Edge Cases
lessons.description: Uncover tricky edge cases: duplicate values, negative numbers, all elements equal, and sorted inputs.

items: Duplicates: `[5, 5, 5, 5]` when searching or sorting.
All Negative Numbers: `[-10, -5, -20]` when finding max subarray sum.
Sorted / Reverse Sorted: `[1, 2, 3, 4]` or `[4, 3, 2, 1]` for QuickSort pivots.
Floating Point Precision: `0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3` in binary floating point representation.

keyTakeaways: Construct edge cases specifically aimed at breaking your algorithm's assumptions.
Ensure Kadane's algorithm handles all negative number arrays.

quiz.question: Why is an array with all negative numbers `[-5, -2, -8]` an edge case for maximum subarray sum?
options: Initializing max_sum to 0 yields wrong answer 0 instead of -2
quiz.explanation: If max_sum is initialized to 0, returning 0 is incorrect because all elements are negative; maximum sum is -2.

lessons.title: C/C++ Debugging
lessons.description: Fix segmentation faults, memory leaks, dangling pointers, and undefined behavior in C/C++.

content.text: A Segmentation Fault (SIGSEGV) occurs when reading or writing restricted RAM memory.

items: Dereferencing NULL pointer: `int *p = nullptr; *p = 10;`
Array index out of bounds.
Stack overflow from deep recursion.

keyTakeaways: Use address sanitizers (`-fsanitize=address`) when compiling C++ locally.
Initialize all raw pointers to `nullptr`.

quiz.question: What causes a Segmentation Fault in C++?
options: Attempting to access unauthorized or unallocated memory
quiz.explanation: SIGSEGV is triggered by illegal memory access, such as dereferencing null or invalid pointers.

lessons.title: Java Debugging
lessons.description: Fix NullPointerExceptions, Integer object equality `==`, and ConcurrentModificationException.

content.title: Integer Caching Bug
content.whyItFails: Java caches Integer objects between -128 and 127. For values >= 128, `==` compares distinct object memory addresses.
content.explanation: Always use `.equals()` for wrapper object value comparisons.

keyTakeaways: Use `.equals()` when comparing Java wrapper objects (`Integer`, `Long`).
Avoid modifying Collection objects while iterating with a standard for-each loop.

quiz.question: In Java, why does `Integer a = 200; Integer b = 200; (a == b)` evaluate to false?
options: `==` compares object references, and 200 is outside Java's -128..127 Integer cache range
quiz.explanation: Java caches Integer objects from -128 to 127. Values outside range create separate objects with different addresses.

lessons.title: Python Debugging
lessons.description: Troubleshoot mutable default arguments, indentation errors, and shallow vs deep copies.

content.title: Default List Parameter Bug

buggyCode.python:
def add_item(item, target_list=[]):  # Bug: target_list shared across all function calls!
    target_list.append(item)
    return target_list

print(add_item(1))  # [1]
print(add_item(2))  # [1, 2] - Unexpected retention!

correctCode.python:
def add_item(item, target_list=None):
    if target_list is None:
        target_list = []
    target_list.append(item)
    return target_list

print(add_item(1))  # [1]
print(add_item(2))  # [2]

content.whyItFails: Default parameter expressions are evaluated ONCE when function is defined, creating a persistent shared list.
content.explanation: Use `None` as default argument and instantiate new list inside function body.

keyTakeaways: Never use mutable default arguments (`[]` or `{}`) in Python function signatures.
Use `copy.deepcopy()` when cloning nested lists.

quiz.question: Why should you avoid `def fn(items=[])` in Python?
options: The default list `[]` is evaluated once at definition time and shared across subsequent function calls
quiz.explanation: Mutable default arguments persist state across multiple function invocations.

lessons.title: JavaScript Debugging
lessons.description: Debug implicit type coercion, asynchronous Promises, `this` binding, and loose equality `==`.

content.title: Loose vs Strict Equality

buggyCode.javascript:
console.log(0 == '0'); // true (type coercion)
console.log([] == false); // true
console.log(null == undefined); // true

correctCode.javascript:
console.log(0 === '0'); // false (strict comparison)
console.log([] === false); // false
console.log(null === undefined); // false

content.whyItFails: Loose equality `==` performs unexpected type conversions before comparing.
content.explanation: Always use strict equality `===` in JavaScript.

keyTakeaways: Always use strict equality `===` and `!==` in JavaScript.
Handle async Promise rejections with `try/catch` in `async/await` functions.

quiz.question: What is the key difference between `==` and `===` in JavaScript?
options: `==` performs type coercion before comparison; `===` checks both value and type strictly
quiz.explanation: Strict equality `===` compares values without performing automatic type coercion.

lessons.title: Print Debugging Techniques

content.code:
#define DEBUG 1
#if DEBUG
    #define debug(x) cout << #x << " = " << x << endl;
#else

#endif

keyTakeaways: Use preprocessor directives or flags to toggle debug logging instantaneously.
Format debug output clearly using label-value pairs.

quiz.question: What is the advantage of using a conditional `DEBUG` flag for logging?
options: It enables toggling all debug messages on/off instantly without deleting lines
quiz.explanation: A single boolean or macro flag toggles all debug logs cleanly across the program.

lessons.title: Variable Tracing & State Diagrams

content.text: For stateful problems (e.g. string parsing, state machines, DP), draw state transition diagrams on paper.

keyTakeaways: Draw state transitions visually when debugging finite state machines.
Track variable mutations across loop boundaries.

quiz.question: When is state diagram visual tracing most valuable?
options: For multi-state parsers, state machines, and dynamic programming transitions
quiz.explanation: Visualizing state machine transitions prevents missing branch state transitions.

lessons.title: Common Debugging Mistakes
lessons.description: Avoid shotgun debugging, assuming working code, and emotional debugging traps.

items: Shotgun Debugging: Randomly changing lines without understanding the underlying issue.
Confirmation Bias: Assuming a function works without actually inspecting its return output.
Ignoring Compiler Warnings: Ignoring warnings about unused variables or uninitialized state.

keyTakeaways: Never make random edits hoping code will magically compile or work.
Always investigate compiler warnings immediately.

quiz.question: What is 'shotgun debugging'?
options: Making random code changes blindly hoping one fixes the problem
Writing unit tests for all functions
quiz.explanation: Shotgun debugging refers to making random, unguided changes without understanding root causes.

sections.title: Debugging Strategy
sections.description: Comprehensive step-by-step checklist and quick reference cheat sheet for exam and interview debugging.

lessons.title: Debugging Checklist
lessons.description: The ultimate 10-step checklist to run through whenever code produces Wrong Answer or TLE.

items.title: Check Array Bounds
items.description: Verify array indices span 0 to N-1.

items.title: Check Data Types & Overflow
items.description: Use 64-bit int (`long long`) if values exceed 2*10^9.

items.title: Check Initialization
items.description: Reset global arrays and variables between test cases.

items.title: Check Loop Termination
items.description: Ensure loop counter increments/decrements towards base case.

items.title: Check Recursion Base Cases
items.description: Verify null/zero checks at top of recursive functions.

items.title: Check Edge Cases
items.description: Test N=0, N=1, negative inputs, and duplicates.

items.title: Check Time Complexity
items.description: Ensure N <= 10^5 uses O(N) or O(N log N).

items.title: Check Memory Allocation
items.description: Ensure static matrix sizes do not exceed ~256MB limit.

items.title: Read Error Messages Carefully
items.description: Read the top-most line of compiler/interpreter error message.

keyTakeaways: Bookmark and run through the 10-step checklist systematically whenever stuck.
Verify data types, bounds, and initializations first.

quiz.question: What is the second item on the universal debugging checklist?
options: Check Data Types & Integer Overflow limits
quiz.explanation: Checking data types and potential integer overflow is a critical early step when debugging wrong answers.

lessons.title: Debugging Cheat Sheet
lessons.description: Quick reference guide for error codes, complexity thresholds, and diagnostic commands.

rows: Read top line of compiler error trace.
Array out of bounds, Null pointer, Divide by 0
Check array indices, pointer null checks, and divisor != 0.
Optimize algorithm or check loop increment statements.
Reduce array size or optimize DP matrix to 1D.
Switch to long long, test edge cases (N=0, N=1, negative).

keyTakeaways: Use verdict quick references to narrow down root causes instantly.
Maintain a structured, calm approach to troubleshooting code errors.

quiz.question: Which immediate fix action corresponds to a Runtime Error (RE)?
options: Optimize algorithm from O(N^2) to O(N)
Check array indexing boundaries, null pointer checks, and division by zero
quiz.explanation: Runtime errors are caused by invalid operations during execution like out-of-bounds indexing, null dereferencing, or division by zero.
